item.content:encoded:
The Tiyan High School campus, which has been closed for repairs since August, passed a sanitation inspection conducted by the Department of Public Health and Social Services.

Guam Department of Education spokesperson Damen Michael Borja said details on the return to campus are still in the planning phase. The department will hold meetings with students, parents and others before making final decisions.

The campus housed students from both Tiyan and Simon Sanchez High Schools when classes began in August, but the facility was closed after failing a sanitation inspection. Eventually, students from Simon Sanchez were sent to Okkodo High School, and students from Tiyan were sent to George Washington High School.

All four schools are conducting split sessions.

Borja said the Tiyan inspection was conducted Tuesday morning and involved all areas except those cordoned off for renovations.

item.title: Guam schools lose WASC accreditation due to outstanding purchase order payment
item.description: Several Guam schools were recently notified that their accreditation was terminated, effective immediately, by the Western Association of Schools and Colleges. The Guam Department of Education did not name the schools that were involved and did not say how many had their accreditation terminated.
item.content:encoded:
Several Guam schools were recently notified that their accreditation was terminated, effective immediately, by the Western Association of Schools and Colleges.

The Guam Department of Education did not name the schools that were involved and did not say how many had their accreditation terminated.

GDOE spokesperson Damen Michael Borja said the termination stems from an outstanding purchase order payment from School Year 2024–2025 that was not processed at the time.

Borja said the department has since addressed the outstanding payment, which was completed Monday.

He said the department is currently awaiting confirmation from WASC regarding accreditation status.

Borja said remains committed to working collaboratively with WASC and will continue efforts to secure the required WASC membership for School Year 2026–2027.

item.title: Community fishing locker installed in Hagåtña Mayor’s Office
item.description: The Department of Agriculture’s Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources, or DAWR, and the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office have installed a community fishing locker at the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office. The gear is available to all Guam residents with a valid form of identification. There is no age restriction, and the equipment includes reels sized for children.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Agriculture’s Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources, or DAWR, and the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office have installed a community fishing locker at the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office.

The gear is available to all Guam residents with a valid form of identification. There is no age restriction, and the equipment includes reels sized for children.

The locker has six rod-and-reel combinations in varying sizes, as well as tackle boxes and fishing tackle.

Adults may borrow equipment for themselves or on behalf of a child or guardian.

Borrowers must provide valid identification, complete a Fishing Locker Checkout Form, and sign a participant agreement. After use, the equipment must be returned to the Hagåtña Mayor’s Office for inspection.

DAWR also offers fishing clinics by appointment for community members interested in hands-on fishing instruction.

The Community Fishing Locker was funded through a grant from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Office of Conservation Investment. DAWR says the program aims to make recreational fishing more accessible while encouraging responsible fishing and stewardship of Guam’s aquatic resources.

item.title: 'Avengers: Endgame' takes the box office crown back from 'Avatar'
item.description: Avengers: Endgame has reclaimed the number one spot on Hollywood's all-time worldwide box office chart. The superhero epic, in which dozens of Marvel superheroes oppose Thanos, a supervillain who has erased half the universe's population, first became the highest grossing film in history in 2019.
item.content:encoded:
Avengers: Endgame has reclaimed the number one spot on Hollywood's all-time worldwide box office chart.

The superhero epic, in which dozens of Marvel superheroes oppose Thanos, a supervillain who has erased half the universe's population, first became the highest grossing film in history in 2019.

Its $2.799 billion total eclipsed that of James Cameron's sci-fi epic Avatar (2009), which had held that title for ten years.

Then Avatar, which tells the story of an Indigenous population fighting off a human invasion on the moon Pandora, was re-released in 2022 to drum up interest in a sequel, Avatar: The Way of Water. That re-release, combined with a first-time release in China, earned enough to allow Avatar to retake the top spot.

Now, it's the Avengers franchise that has a sequel coming — Avengers: Doomsday , arriving in theaters on December 18. So, following the same playbook, Endgame has been re-released, and has reclaimed the crown with a new worldwide total of $2.9255 billion.

It's a friendly competition — both films are Disney releases. And while those numbers are impressive, their jockeying reflects rising ticket prices more than rising attendance.

item.title: What to know about nationwide protests in India over voter list changes
item.description: NEW DELHI — Protests have spread across India in the past week as opposition parties and civil society groups demand the resignation of the country's election chief over alleged manipulation of voter lists. The campaign has been led in part by India's "Cockroach" youth movement, which previously organized street protests that forced the education minister to resign in July.
item.content:encoded:
NEW DELHI — Protests have spread across India in the past week as opposition parties and civil society groups demand the resignation of the country's election chief over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

The campaign has been led in part by India's "Cockroach" youth movement, which previously organized street protests that forced the education minister to resign in July.

Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the poll body's ongoing revision of voter lists. They accuse the revision could disenfranchise millions of voters and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP. The commission and government deny any wrongdoing.

India is the world's largest democracy with hundreds of millions of people voting in national and state elections. The Election Commission plays a central role in determining voter eligibility and administering elections, making changes to electoral lists politically significant.

The dispute centers on a nationwide voter list revision known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR. It began last year in the eastern state of Bihar ahead of local elections and has since expanded to most of India's states and federally administered territories.

Under the process, voters are required to provide documents showing they are eligible to remain on the lists.

The Election Commission says the exercise is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible entries and ensure legitimate voters remain registered. Critics say it could instead exclude legitimate voters, particularly poorer and other vulnerable communities.

They also say the requirements are confusing and difficult for many people to provide, particularly those who lack older government records or other documents.

India's Election Commission is an independent constitutional body overseeing elections and maintaining voter lists, but opposition parties accuse the commission of favoring Modi's party. They allege the changes could remove people more likely to support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters who favor the BJP.

The BJP and the Election Commission reject the allegations and say the revision has no political motive. Modi's party says the list is being updated to weed out what they call "infiltrators."

The issue was prominent in West Bengal's crucial state elections earlier this year after a voter list revision removed about 9 million names, or roughly 12% of the electorate. The deletions left millions of eligible voters unable to cast ballots. Modi's party won the state for the first time.

Indian law requires a majority vote of commission members to enact changes making disagreements among its members potentially significant.

The Indian Express newspaper reported in September that two of the three election commissioners had formally objected to several decisions involving voter list revisions, registration procedures and the commission's digital systems.

The newspaper reported Kumar, the election chief, rejected those objections.

The Election Commission said the report reflected "differing views and deliberations" rather than formal written objections.

The "Cockroach" movement, opposition parties and civil society groups have called for Kumar to resign or be removed and for an inquiry into his conduct, including possible criminal proceedings. They want the current revision halted and the previous electoral lists used for future elections.

They also demand a more independent and transparent process for appointing election commissioners.

Election Commission data indicates voter lists in some regions could shrink by as much as 30%, fueling concerns among opposition parties and protest groups over potential exclusions.

The dispute is likely to intensify as the changes resulting from the revision expand throughout India, which is facing a series of state elections early next year.

item.title: Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat
item.description: HANOI, Vietnam — Police in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, Vietnamese state media said. Police identified 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh as the alleged leader of the network. He and 11 others were being investigated for theft, state media said Monday.
item.content:encoded:
HANOI, Vietnam — Police in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, Vietnamese state media said.

Police identified 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh as the alleged leader of the network. He and 11 others were being investigated for theft, state media said Monday.

Investigators said Binh bought stolen cats, kept them at a facility in the city's north and resold them for meat. He worked with suppliers who recruited others to ride motorcycles through residential neighborhoods between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., hunting for cats and trapping four to 10 cats each night.

Eating dog and cat meat is not unique to Vietnam and has been practiced in parts of Asia, though it is not common practice. In Vietnam, cat meat traditionally is more commonly consumed in the north, among older generations.

The practice has declined with growing pet ownership and urbanization, and younger Vietnamese are more likely to regard dogs and cats as companion animals.

In 2024, more than 250,000 people signed a petition calling for an end to Vietnam's dog and cat meat trade. The city of Hoi An also pledged in 2021 to end the sale and consumption of dog and cat meat.

Some believe eating cat meat brings good luck, though there is no scientific evidence for such claims.

Police raided the network on July 8 and found about 50 cats and dozens of traps, state media reported.

The suspects told investigators they had stolen and sold about 2,700 cats, the reports said. Police did not say how long the operation had been running.

Police returned 13 of the cats confiscated in the raid to their owners. A nonprofit animal rights group was caring for the others while authorities sought to identify their owners.

Under Vietnamese law, dogs and cats are considered private property, and stealing them is considered theft. Criminal prosecution generally applies when the value of the stolen property exceeds 2 million dong ($77).

In a separate raid in June, police reported they had rescued more than 400 cats. At least 40 were reunited with their owners, but dozens of dead cats were found packed in ice.

item.title: A history of presidents naming things after themselves (It's short. They rarely do)

item.content:encoded:
President Trump recently underscored his desire to have his name appear on the facade of the Kennedy Center with a threat. "Frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump told reporters. "It'll end up being ripped down."

Trump or his supporters have called for the president's name to appear on everything from naval battleships to airports . It's pretty rare for sitting presidents to stamp their identities on infrastructure, currency and other public assets — though history shows there are a few exceptions.

Discussions regarding this issue go all the way back to the first presidential administration.

"They were trying to figure out what was the right balance between the prestige required to give this new office respect, but also recognizing that they were not trying to re-create a monarchy," said Lindsay Chervinsky , executive director of the George Washington Presidential Library and author of The Cabinet: George Washington and the Creation of an American Institution .

Chervinsky said the issue first came up at the federal level during Washington's presidency around the Coinage Act of 1792. Congress was figuring out what to put on the inaugural American coins, given the habit in Great Britain and other nations of plastering the reigning monarch all over theirs.

"The House of Representatives said that the president should not be on currency because of this monarchical tie," Chervinsky said.

Chervinsky said Washington shared their concerns. The president usually shied away from ostentatious self-celebration. "He didn't want a lot of fuss," she said.

But sometimes, Washington didn't seem to mind it. "They did name the federal city Washington to honor him while he was still in office," Chervinsky said.

Most administrations have generally kept the names and faces of sitting presidents off public assets since then, viewing it as unseemly.

On the few occasions when a sitting president's name has appeared — such as on dams named for Teddy Roosevelt , Calvin Coolidge and Woodrow Wilson — it tended not to be the man in office pushing for it himself. "Usually it is political supporters," Chervinsky said. And the history around the naming process can be fraught.

The most prominent example of this is the Hoover Dam.

The massive public works project located near the Boulder Canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border had been known in the early stages of its development as the Boulder Dam . Hoover's secretary of the interior, Ray Lyman Wilbur, suggested rechristening the project in 1930 as the Hoover Dam, owing to the lead role Hoover had played in its planning. "Hoover negotiated the deal among the states known as the Colorado River Compact that allocated the river's water among seven states," said Kenneth Whyte, author of Hoover: An Extraordinary Life in Extraordinary Times . "So it was generally agreed that it was deserved."

Apparently, the president thought so too. "Hoover, I think, was pleased about it," said Whyte. "But he did not talk a lot about it at the time. He didn't want to be seen to be doing self-aggrandizing things."

But the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration was having none of it. After Roosevelt took office in 1933, his secretary of the interior, Harold Ickes, called for the dam to revert to its original moniker.

"Ickes based this argument on the fact that the original legislation that authorized Congress to fund the project was called the Boulder Canyon Project Act," said Marist University's David Woolner, a senior fellow and resident historian at the Roosevelt Institute, and the author of several books about the 32nd U.S. president. "And he did not like the politics of Herbert Hoover."

Woolner said Roosevelt did not object to the change. He kept his political rival's name out of his 1935 dedication speech, consistently referring to it as "Boulder Dam."

Although there was some initial opposition from Democrats, in 1947, Congress voted unanimously to change the name back . Woolner said this happened "in recognition of Hoover's early support for the project, and after the former president gained praise for his humanitarian work during and after the First and Second World Wars."

Roosevelt, for his part, wasn't "particularly anxious to have things named after him," Woolner said.

But that didn't stop Roosevelt from lending his name to one major project during his presidency — the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum — "which of course he initiated," said Woolner.

In keeping with this tradition, President Trump told reporters at a press briefing earlier this year he is planning to build himself a presidential library in Miami.

Except it probably won't be a library. And presidential libraries are, technically speaking, public-private assets.

"I don't believe in building libraries or museums," Trump said. "But it's most likely going to be a hotel with a beautiful building underneath and a 747 Air Force One in the lobby."

One thing that seems certain, judging by a video rendering on the president's social media channel promoting the project: Trump's name will be prominently displayed on its facade.
